query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ build-plate preheating, optimized in real time via a machine learning model integrating thermal feedback, reduces the thermal gradients during additive manufacturing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, thereby minimizing compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation and ultimately improving mechanical integrity relative to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy produced from powder feedstock using conventional additive manufacturing methods, which typically exhibit rapid cooling-induced segregation, high residual thermal stresses, and notable defect formation.
generation.intervention: Implement an in-situ build-plate preheating strategy, with the preheat temperature continuously optimized via a machine learning model that uses real-time thermal feedback to adjust processing parameters during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: Valid during laser-based additive manufacturing processing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi under conditions with rapid solidification and significant thermal gradients; comparison is made against a baseline using a room-temperature build plate under identical power and scan settings.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform temperature distribution across the melt pool and adjacent regions reduces the thermal gradients during solidification, which in turn limits elemental segregation, alleviates residual thermal stresses, and minimizes defect formation in the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build plate decreases the temperature differential between the melt pool and the substrate, slowing down the cooling rate and promoting more homogeneous solidification. The machine learning model fine-tunes the preheat temperature in real time to adapt to process variations, thereby reducing stress concentrations and defects that compromise mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy is expected to exhibit improved mechanical integrity, with reductions in compositional segregation and residual stresses, as well as a lower defect density compared to conventionally fabricated samples. Directionally, one would observe enhanced tensile strength and ductility, although the exact magnitude of improvement is subject to further experimental quantification.
generation.baseline: Conventional additive manufacturing processing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi using a room-temperature build plate with standard laser parameters.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in laser powder bed fusion or comparable AM processes under rapid solidification conditions. Effects outside typical AM processing regimes or in processes with inherently low thermal gradients remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is plausible based on thermal management principles and prior trends in additive manufacturing, the precise quantitative improvements in stress reduction and defect minimization are not yet defined and must be validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment where identical cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock is processed using laser powder bed fusion in two setups: one with a conventional room-temperature build plate and one with an in-situ preheated build plate whose temperature is optimized in real time via a machine learning algorithm. Both samples will be fabricated using the same laser power, scan strategy, and layer thickness.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to quantify compositional segregation and defect density
Residual stress measurement using X-ray diffraction or equivalent techniques
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) to evaluate strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in-situ preheated, ML-optimized sample does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both compositional segregation and residual stresses, as well as no improvement in mechanical performance compared to the conventional sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

decision.trend: Early studies first attempted to gain improved mechanical integrity in high‐entropy alloys by tweaking alloy compositions and using conventional bulk processes. In additive manufacturing of HEAs, process‐induced challenges became apparent – rapid solidification led to refined microstructures but also to pronounced compositional segregation, residual thermal stresses and defect formation. Subsequent works using laser powder bed fusion and related techniques experimented with altered laser energy inputs, remelting strategies, and scan patterns to lessen these effects. Although grain size refinement and phase control were achieved, the fundamental thermal gradients between melt and substrate remained a persistent source of residual stress and segregation.
decision.unsolved: Even with adjustments in composition and traditional process parameters, the rapid cooling intrinsic to current additive manufacturing methods continues to induce nonuniform elemental distribution (segregation) and high residual stresses that compromise mechanical integrity. A method simultaneously reducing segregation, thermal gradients, and defect formation without altering the alloy composition is still missing.
decision.lever: Implement an in-situ build-plate preheating strategy optimized via a machine learning model that integrates real-time thermal feedback with processing parameters
decision.why: The trend shows that while conventional laser parameter adjustments partially mitigate defects, the dominant issue remains the extreme thermal gradients during rapid solidification. A single intervention that actively controls the substrate temperature – thereby reducing cooling rates and thermal contraction stresses – is a promising next step. Using a data‐driven or machine learning model to optimize and precisely control the build-plate preheat temperature leverages recent advances in process monitoring and model‐based optimization. This approach is expected to quantitatively minimize compositional segregation and residual stress relative to conventional AM or bulk processing techniques, and it naturally conforms with the additive manufacturing regimes already in use for cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi.
